hints: Speed gained on one half must be lost on the other, over the same length. What does that say about the two accelerations?
worded:
1. On the smooth half the body speeds up at g sin φ; on the rough half it must slow down by the same amount over the same length.

2. Equal lengths and equal changes in v² mean equal and opposite accelerations: g(μ cos φ − sin φ) = g sin φ.

3. So μ cos φ = 2 sin φ, μ = 2 tan φ. (C)

4. Energy check: gravity does work over the whole length; friction only over half, so it must be twice gravity’s component.

**Another way: work–energy.** From rest to rest: mg sin φ × L = μmg cos φ × L/2, so μ = 2 tan φ.
conventional:
![](asset:P000556-sol-1)

Each half has length $L/2$. Work–energy from rest at the top to rest at the bottom:

$$mg\sin\varphi\, L - \mu mg\cos\varphi\,\frac{L}{2} = 0\mkern6mu  \Rightarrow \mkern6mu \mu = 2\tan\varphi.$$
mistakes: Friction acts only on half the length, so μ is twice tan φ, not tan φ.
